Julius II. Reigning from 1503 to 1513, Julius II was one of the most powerful, active, and influential popes of the High Renaissance. Known as the Warrior Pope, he personally led military campaigns to expand the Papal States and restore church authority in Italy. Equally formidable as a diplomat and cultural force, he transformed Rome into the artistic capital of Europe by commissioning some of the most famous works of art in human history.

He earned the nickname Warrior Pope for personally donning armor and leading papal troops to conquer Bologna, Perugia, and the Romagna region. In 1506, he established the Swiss Guard, recruiting mercenary soldiers from Switzerland to serve as the permanent papal security force and personal bodyguard. In 1508, he organized the League of Cambrai with France and the Holy Roman Empire to strip the Republic of Venice of its mainland Italian territories. He later formed the Holy League in 1511 to drive French troops out of northern Italy, successfully forming an alliance with Spain, England, and the Holy Roman Empire.

In 1506, Julius began the rebuilding of St. Peter's Basilica, laying the foundation stone for the massive new structure designed by Donato Bramante. He commissioned Michelangelo to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512, forcing the sculptor to paint a vast fresco cycle of Old Testament scenes. He commissioned Raphael to decorate the Stanze di Raffaello in the Apostolic Palace, which resulted in famous Renaissance masterpieces like The School of Athens. He also commissioned Michelangelo to sculpt a monumental tomb for himself, a project that was never finished as originally planned but yielded the famous horned statue of Moses. His massive architectural projects were funded partly by the sale of indulgences, which set the stage for the religious upheavals of the Protestant Reformation.
